div.head: Geþyncðo 1
div.ab: Hwilum wæs . . ., þæt leod ⁊ lagu fór be geþingðum; ⁊ þá wæron þeodwitan wurðscipes wurðe, ælc be his mæðe, ge eorl ge ceorl, ge þegen ge þeoden.
Hit wæs hwilum on Engla lagum, þæt leod ⁊ lagu for be geþincðum; ⁊ þa wæron leodwítan weorðscipes wyrðe, ælc be his mæðe, eorl ⁊ ceorl, þegen ⁊ þeoden.
Aliquando fuit in Anglorum laga, quod populus et leges consilio regebantur; et tunc erant sapientes populi magni prorsus nominis et pretii, comes et uillanus, tainus et alii singuli pro modo suo.
[60] Antiqua lex Anglorum fuit, quod gens illorúm et consuetudines in honore tenebantur; et per consilium dabantur (uni-) cuique secundum mensuram cuiusque comiti et uillano, liberali et subliberali.
Hit wæs hwilum on Engla lagum þæt leod and lagu for be geþincðum, and þa wæron leodwitan weorðscipes wyrðe, ælc be his mæðe, eorl and ceorl, þegen and þeoden.

Einst galt es in Engländer-Rechten, dass Volk und Berechtigung gemäss Würden ging; und da genossen die Rathsherren der Nation Ehre, jeder nach seinem Rang, so Adliger wie Gemeiner, so Dienstritter wie Fürst (A. und G., D. und F. H).

Once it was in the laws of the English that people and law went by rank [were ordered]; and then the counsellors of the nation enjoyed honour, each according to his rank, noble as well as commoner, thegn as well as prince (n. and c., t. and p., H).
Once it used to be that people and rights went by dignities, and councillors of the people were then entitled to honour, each according to his rank, whether noble or ceorl, retainer or lord.

In the laws of the English, it once was that people and law were ordered by status, and the people’s councilors were treated with dignity, each according to his rank, noble and commoner, thane and lord.
div.note: D lacks ‘on Engla lagum’ (Liebermann supplies it from the others). ‘þeoden’ is poetic, so the Quadripartitus and Instituta misunderstood it (as in Beowulf 2722, 2869). ‘eorl ⁊ ceorl’ is a rhyming pair, ‘þegen ⁊ þeoden’ alliterating. Another late compiler begins two sentences the same way (Grið 3, 22).; AZ: corrected against Rabin p. 10 / 11, October 2026 (was “∅”, now “|”); AT: corrected against Whitelock p. 476, October 2026 (was “egen; eoden.; egen”, now “þegen; þeoden.; þegen”)
eorl . . . þeoden: ge eorl ge ceorl, ge þegen ge þeoden D
people and law were ordered by status: The word geþincðu lacks a direct modern English equivalent, and it previously has been translated as “rank,” “status,” “dignity,” and “honor.”
thane: A landowner lower in status than a lord, with military obligations to his superior.

note.seg: die Sprache des Stücks ist mehrfach durch Rhythmus und Alliteration gehoben. Regelmässige Verse aber ergeben nur die ersten Zeilen. Sonstiges zwängt in Verse Leo Rectitudines 108 nur mit Gewalt und unvollkommen. — Weil Schrift und meistentheils Lautstand älter in D als in H, steht hier D links; Thorpe’s Text ruht auf H. Allerdings lässt D, wie gewöhnlich, Sätze fort, ändert in klerikaler Tendenz, überspringt und modernisirt bisweilen auch Stil und Laute gegenüber dem Archetyp von H, Quadr. und Inst.

the language of the piece is raised in several places by rhythm and alliteration. Only the first lines, however, yield regular verse. Leo, Rectitudines 108, forces the rest into verse only by violence and imperfectly. — Because the script and for the most part the phonology are older in D than in H, D is placed here on the left; Thorpe’s text is based on H. D, to be sure, as usual, omits sentences, makes alterations with a clerical tendency, skips, and sometimes also modernises style and sounds as against the archetype of H, Quadr. and Inst.

‘in Engländer-Rechten’, obwohl D fehlend, ist archetyp, weil vorhanden in Inst und der anderen Hss.-Klasse hq.—Im Ggs. zur Dena lagu wird auch Engla lagu nur im Sing. gebraucht; diese Bed. liegt also hier nicht vor.—Über die Bedeutung des Tempus der Vergangenheit in diesem Stücke s. o. Einl. 10.—Leod übs. unrichtig ‘Wergeld’ Phillips Agsä. RG. 115; dagegen Grimm DRA. 267

‘In the laws of the English’, although missing in D, belongs to the archetype, since it is present in Inst and in the other class of MSS, hq.—When contrasted with the Dena lagu, Engla lagu too is used only in the sing.; that meaning, therefore, is not present here.—On the significance of the past tense in this piece see above Introduction 10.—Phillips Agsä. RG. 115 incorrectly translates Leod as ‘wergild’; against this, Grimm DRA. 267
= sich richtete

fór kann nicht Präposition (Wilkins, Phillips) sein, da von D akzentuiert, und da Präp. folgt. Bed. von faran ebenso Episc 6
fór cannot be a preposition (Wilkins, Phillips), since D accents it, and since a preposition follows. The meaning of faran is the same in Episc 6

‘Angesehene im Volke’ Grimm, zu allgemein. Gewiss ist die Nationalversammlung darunter mitgemeint, doch vielleicht nicht im Ggs. (wie Price meint) zu scirwitan. Das Laienhafte allein, im Ggs. zum Klerus (wie Phillips meint), liegt in dem Worte nicht.—þeod ist mit leod synonym und steht in derselben Hs. D, wo der andere Text leod liest, auch V Atr 2. Vgl. über die Composita mein National assembly p. 7³

‘Men of standing among the people’ Grimm: too general. The national assembly is certainly included in the meaning, but perhaps not in contrast (as Price thinks) to scirwitan. The lay character alone, in contrast to the clergy (as Phillips thinks), does not lie in the word.—þeod is synonymous with leod and also stands in V Atr 2 in the same MS D, where the other text reads leod. On the compounds cf. my National assembly p. 7³
rhyming pair
S. ebd. 37¹; villanus bei Q meint noch nicht einen Unfreien
See ibid. 37¹; villanus in Q does not yet mean an unfree man

Q setzt für þeoden falsch einen allgemeinen, Inst gar einen fast entgegengesetzten Begriff; denn subliberalis meint doch wohl ‘weniger, nur etwas, minder frei’. Dachte er an die in Poesie ebenfalls vorhandene Floskel þegn ⁊ þeow (Phönix 165)?

Q wrongly puts a general concept for þeoden, and Inst even an almost opposite one; for subliberalis surely means ‘less, only somewhat, less fully free’. Was he thinking of the phrase þegn ⁊ þeow (Phönix 165), likewise found in poetry?
alliterating pair

note.label: rights
note.seg: leod and lagu. In alliterative and rhymed formulas words may be used in a vague or archaic sense. “Law” here is used to cover all the complex of rights and obligations of each rank.

note.label: lord
note.seg: ge eorl ge ceorl, ge þegen ge þeoden. Here eorl retains its old sense of “noble” and þegen the element of service rather than of rank.
